title: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Distinct southern genera spread from a once-vegetated Antarctica before the Glacial period

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Distinct species of genera confined to the southern hemisphere spread in radiating lines from the antarctic lands, which supported a peculiar flora during a warmer period before the Glacial period, reaching southern America, Australia and New Zealand by occasional transport and former islands.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I am inclined to look in the southern, as in the northern hemisphere, to a former and warmer period, before the commencement of the Glacial period, when the antarctic lands, now covered with ice, supported a highly peculiar and isolated flora.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XI, “Geographical Distribution”; section “Dispersal during the Glacial period co-extensive with the world”. Scope: southern-hemisphere plant genera with disjunct distributions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch11-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The historical scenario has testable fossil and phylogenetic predictions for many genera. Sparse Antarctic evidence and alternative Gondwanan histories prevent full resolution as a general mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For southern disjunct plant genera, infer ancestral areas and divergence dates and compare them with Antarctic fossils, paleoclimate, and changing island connections. Support requires Antarctic ancestry during a warm preglacial interval followed by outward lineage splits.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Antarctic terrestrial fossil sampling is sparse.

Vicariance can mimic radiating dispersal.

Divergence estimates may not identify former stepping-stone islands.

fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.79
data existence: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.59
discriminating power: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Antarctic fossils and southern ranges exist in public databases, and trees exist for many of the classic disjunct genera. Together they can test an Antarctic connection for a subset of genera. Date uncertainty and the thin fossil flora leave continental breakup and overseas dispersal as live alternatives for most clades.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Combine pre-glacial Antarctic fossil plants with phylogenies of southern-hemisphere disjunct genera and ask whether those genera connect through an Antarctic source older than the glacial period. Roots centered only on Australia or South America, with no Antarctic fossil link, would count against the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Continental breakup, later dispersal, and an Antarctic source are hard to separate when divergence dates are uncertain.

The Antarctic macrofossil flora is small and geographically narrow.
